adhikaram.english: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)

kurals.tamil:
இருநோக்கு இவளுண்கண் உள்ளது ஒருநோக்கு
நோய்நோக்கொன் றந்நோய் மருந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Irunokku ivalunkan ulladhu orunokku
noinokkon randhnoi marundhu.
kurals.meaning: Her darkened eyes hold two kinds of look: one look gives me the ache of love, and the other is the very medicine for that ache.
kurals.elementary: Think of a new classmate who is very shy. When she looks at you, you feel all fluttery and nervous inside. But when she looks again and gives a small friendly smile, the nervous feeling goes away. The same eyes made the worry and then made it better.
kurals.university: Chapter 110 opens the second stage of the kalaviyal (the section on secret, premarital love): after the first sight of ch. 109 (Takaiyananguruttal), the hero now reads the heroine’s kurippu (குறிப்பு, ‘sign, inward intention’) for proof that his love is returned. The chapter shares its title with ch. 71 of Porutpal, where kurippu arithal means reading a king’s mind, so the same art of reading the face is moved from the court to love. Unkan (உண்கண்) means eyes that have ‘eaten’ collyrium (mai), that is, kohl-darkened eyes, and every gloss on both source sites (Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesikan, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) reads the two looks as a nōy nōkku (நோய் நோக்கு, the look that causes love-sickness) and a remedy-look; in the line of Parimelazhagar the second look is her answering sign of consent, which ends his uncertainty. Pope renders: ‘A double witchery have glances of her liquid eye; / One glance is glance that brings me pain; the other heals again.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A remedy is being applied and it will soon be better. It is plain, sir, that you and she love each other.”
hinduism.explanation: When King Dushyanta asks whether Shakuntala’s illness is dangerous, her friend Priyamvada smiles and tells him the cure is already at hand, because the sickness is love for him.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the one who caused the love-sickness is also its medicine.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act III (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the Project Gutenberg text of Ryder’s translation; the illness-and-remedy idea matches, though here a friend speaks rather than a glance.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Turn away thine eyes from me, for they have overcome me.”
christianity.explanation: The lover in the Song of Songs begs the beloved to look away because her gaze overwhelms him.
christianity.tie_back: The beloved’s eyes have the same power to wound the lover that the Kural’s first look has.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); it matches the wounding look but has no second, healing look.

islam.explanation: The women of the city say that the sight of Joseph has filled the wife of al-Aziz with a love she cannot master.
islam.tie_back: The Qur’an too knows that the mere sight of a person can strike the heart with love like an illness, though it judges this love as error.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified via the quran.com API; only the idea of overwhelming love from sight matches, and the Qur’anic context condemns it, so this is a next-best match.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Stay ye me with dainties, refresh me with apples; For I am love-sick.”
judaism.explanation: The maiden in the Song of Songs says she is sick with love and asks to be revived.
judaism.tie_back: Love as a sickness that longs for its own remedy is the image at the heart of the Kural.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; close on love-sickness and its cure, though the cure is not a glance.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that affection itself breeds sorrow and fear, and that freedom from it ends both.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism agrees that love brings an ache, but it finds the cure in letting go of attachment rather than in the beloved’s second look.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it shares the idea that love wounds but rejects the Kural’s romantic remedy, so the match is partial.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The mind of those who always live in unfrequented lodgings, who eat low food, and who subdue their senses, will not be attacked by the foe, Love, who is vanquished as disease is by medicine.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira’s teaching calls love an enemy that can be beaten the way medicine beats a disease, by self-restraint.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism also speaks of love as a sickness with a medicine, but its medicine is restraint of the senses, not the beloved’s answering look.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the disease-and-medicine image is shared, but the Jain cure is renunciation, the opposite of the Kural’s.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “From whose eyes as they glanced flowed love that unnerves the limbs: and beautiful is their glance beneath their brows.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod says that love pours from the glances of the Graces and weakens whoever receives it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, Hesiod places the source of love’s power in a glance of the eyes.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on theoi.com; strong on the glance as the source of love’s weakness, with no healing look.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Phaedrus Socrates describes the lover’s soul as aching and stinging when apart from the beloved, and finding relief from its pangs as soon as it looks on the beloved’s beauty again.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato the sight of the beloved both causes the soul’s agony of longing and soothes it.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s double look: the same beauty gives the pain and the cure.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from the dialogue, since the Jowett text could not be fully loaded to verify exact wording; the thematic match is close.

adhikaram.english: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)

kurals.tamil:
கண்களவு கொள்ளும் சிறுநோக்கம் காமத்தில்
செம்பாகம் அன்று பெரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Kankalavu kollum sirunokkam kaamaththil
sempaakam andru peridhu.
kurals.meaning: The quick glance she steals at me when I am not looking is not merely half of love’s joy; it is more than half.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever caught a friend secretly peeking at the drawing you were making, and then looking away? That tiny peek tells you they really like it, maybe even more than if they had said so out loud. A small secret look can say a lot.
kurals.university: Kan kalavu kollum (கண் களவு கொள்ளும்) is literally ‘the eye that steals’: a look taken by stealth (kalavu, the same word that names the whole kalavu, or secret-love, phase). Ciru nōkkam (சிறுநோக்கம்) is the brief, narrowed glance, which Puliyur Kesikan glosses as arukiya nōkkam, a sparing look cast without his knowledge. Sempākam (செம்பாகம்) means ‘exact half’; the commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar: nērpāti anru, atai vida periya pakuti) agree the stolen glance is greater than half of kāmam, the joy of union, because it reveals that his love is returned. Pope: ‘The furtive glance, that gleams one instant bright, / Is more than half of love’s supreme delight.’ No textual variants appear on the two source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “(She casts a lingering glance at the king, and goes out with her two friends.)”
hinduism.explanation: As Shakuntala leaves her first meeting with King Dushyanta, she makes an excuse to linger and looks back at him.
hinduism.tie_back: Her lingering backward look is exactly the kind of small, stolen sign the Kural says is worth more than half of love.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act I, stage direction (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Project Gutenberg; a stage direction rather than a teaching, but a direct dramatic parallel.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my spouse; thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes.”
christianity.explanation: The lover says a single glance from the beloved has captured his heart.
christianity.tie_back: One look accomplishes almost everything, which is the Kural’s claim about the brief stolen glance.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); near one-to-one on the power of a single glance.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do not give a second look, Ali, (because) while you are not to blame for the first, you have no right to the second.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet tells Ali that an unplanned first glance carries no blame, but he must not follow it with a deliberate second look.
islam.tie_back: Islam, like the Kural, treats a single glance as weighty, but it counsels restraint where the Kural celebrates the glance between future spouses.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 2149 (graded hasan by al-Albani)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; it shares the focus on the brief glance but takes the opposite ethical stance.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Young man, please lift up your eyes and see what you choose for yourself for a wife.”
judaism.explanation: On the joyous fifteenth of Av, the daughters of Jerusalem danced in the vineyards and invited young men to look and choose a bride.
judaism.tie_back: The Mishnah gives the glance a real place at the start of courtship, as the Kural does.
judaism.source: Mishnah Ta’anit 4:8 (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; it values the courtship glance but goes on to tell the young man to look past beauty, and it is not a stolen glance.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Lord, as I was leaving home, a Sakyan girl–the envy of the countryside–glanced up at me, with her hair half-combed, and said, ‘Hurry back, master.’”
buddhism.explanation: Nanda tells the Buddha he cannot keep up the monk’s life because he keeps remembering the glance of the girl he left behind.
buddhism.tie_back: One brief glance outweighed everything else for Nanda, just as the Kural says the small stolen look is more than half of love.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on dhammatalks.org; a strong parallel on the glance’s power, though the sutta uses it to show the pull Nanda must overcome.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is passionately fond of ‘colours,’ will come to untimely ruin; just as an impassioned moth which is attracted by the light rushes into death.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira warns that being captured by what the eye sees leads to ruin, like a moth drawn into a flame.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism agrees with the Kural that what the eye catches can seize the whole heart, but it sees this as danger rather than delight.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a contrasting next-best match, since Jain teaching treats visual attraction as bondage.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “And the maiden looked at him with stealthy glance, holding her bright veil aside, her heart smouldering with pain.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Medea, struck by love for Jason, watches him leave her father’s hall with a secret look from behind her veil.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s kan kalavu, the eye that steals a look, almost word for word.
greek_mythology.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 3.444-446 (tr. R. C. Seaton, 1912)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on theoi.com; near one-to-one on the stolen glance, though Jason does not see it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says that goodwill is the beginning of friendship in the way that the pleasure of the eye is the beginning of love, since no one falls in love without first being delighted by the beloved’s appearance.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, love begins with the pleasure of seeing.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural goes further, saying that one glance is already more than half of love.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.5, 1167a (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, because the online Ross text could not be loaded to verify wording; thematically sound.

adhikaram.english: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)

kurals.tamil:
நோக்கினாள் நோக்கி இறைஞ்சினாள் அஃதவள்
யாப்பினுள் அட்டிய நீர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nokkinaal nokki irainjinaal aqdhaval
yaappinul attiya neer.
kurals.meaning: She looked at me, and having looked, she bowed her head; that gesture was water poured on the growing plant of our love.
kurals.elementary: Imagine planting a seed with a friend. Every time you water it, it grows a little. When someone shyly looks at you and then looks down with a little smile, it is like giving water to the seed of a new friendship.
kurals.university: Iraiñcināḷ (இறைஞ்சினாள்) means ‘she bowed, lowered her head’, the classic sign of nāṇam (நாணம், maidenly modesty) that the hero reads as consent. The key image is yāppu (யாப்பு), which the commentators take as the bond or bed of love: Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as the love she is nurturing, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar as the ‘crop’ (payir) of love, and Puliyur Kesikan as the anpup-payir watered by her sign. Aṭṭiya nīr (அட்டிய நீர்) is water poured into a channel or plot, an agricultural metaphor in keeping with the marutam landscape of settled love. Pope: ‘She looked, and looking drooped her head: / On springing shoot of love ’tis water shed!’ The text is the same on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “(SHAKUNTALA darts a glance at him, then looks down.)”
hinduism.explanation: In Act III, when the king speaks tenderly to her, Shakuntala glances at him and then lowers her eyes.
hinduism.tie_back: The glance followed by the lowered head is exactly the sequence the Kural describes as watering love.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act III, stage direction (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Project Gutenberg; near one-to-one gesture, from a different classical Indian love tradition.

christianity.quote_or_event: “O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely.”
christianity.explanation: The lover calls the shy beloved, hidden like a dove, to show her face.
christianity.tie_back: The beloved’s shy hiding, which only deepens the lover’s longing, is close to the Kural’s modest bowed head.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); it shares the shyness theme but not the look-then-bow gesture.

islam.quote_or_event: “Then one of the two women came to him walking with shyness.”
islam.explanation: The daughter of the old man of Midian approaches Moses with modesty, and the meeting leads to their marriage.
islam.tie_back: Her shyness on meeting Moses is the same nāṇam that the Kural reads as a hopeful sign of love.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified via the quran.com API; a strong parallel on modest shyness leading to marriage.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Raising her eyes, Rebekah saw Isaac. She alighted from the camel and said to the servant, ‘Who is that man walking in the field toward us?’ And the servant said, ‘That is my master.’ So she took her veil and covered herself.”
judaism.explanation: Rebekah lifts her eyes, sees her future husband, and then modestly covers herself with her veil.
judaism.tie_back: She looks, then veils herself: the same pairing of a glance and modest withdrawal that the Kural describes.
judaism.source: Genesis 24:64-65 (THE JPS TANAKH: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; near one-to-one on look-then-modest-withdrawal before a marriage.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Buddhist story of the past life of Gotama, the young ascetic Sumedha meets the maiden Sumitta, who gives him lotuses for the Buddha Dipankara on condition that she may be his companion in future lives.
buddhism.explanation: Their bond begins in one small exchange at a meeting and grows across lifetimes.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s watered shoot, a single modest gesture becomes the seed of a lasting love.
buddhism.source: Jataka Nidanakatha (story of Sumedha and Dipankara)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested story (the maiden’s name differs in other versions); the link to the bowed head is loose.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the crane is produced from an egg, and the egg is produced from a crane, so they call desire the origin of delusion, and delusion the origin of desire.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain scripture says that desire and delusion keep feeding each other in a cycle.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism sees the same self-feeding growth the Kural praises in watered love, but it judges it as a cycle to be broken.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; only the idea of love feeding its own growth matches, in a contrasting frame.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “And ever she kept darting bright glances straight up at Aeson’s son, and within her breast her heart panted fast through anguish, all remembrance left her, and her soul melted with the sweet pain.”
greek_mythology.explanation: After Eros’ arrow strikes her, Medea keeps glancing at Jason as love takes root in her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Her repeated glances show love taking hold and growing, as the Kural’s watered shoot does.
greek_mythology.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 3.286-289 (tr. R. C. Seaton, 1912)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on theoi.com; it matches love growing through glances but lacks the bowed head.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Stendhal compares the growth of love to a bare branch left in a Salzburg salt mine, which comes out covered in sparkling crystals; each small sign from the beloved adds new crystals to the lover’s idea of her.
philosophy.explanation: His theory of ‘crystallization’ explains how love grows from small signs and impressions.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s image of a look as water on a young plant describes the same growth of love from a small sign.
philosophy.source: Stendhal, On Love (De l’amour, 1822), Book I, ch. 2
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Stendhal’s well-known crystallization passage, not verified verbatim this session.

adhikaram.english: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)

kurals.tamil:
யான்நோக்கும் காலை நிலன்நோக்கும் நோக்காக்கால்
தான்நோக்கி மெல்ல நகும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Yaannokkum kaalai nilannokkum nokkaakkaal
thaannokki mella nagum.
kurals.meaning: When I look at her, she looks at the ground; when I do not look, she looks at me and smiles softly to herself.
kurals.elementary: Picture a shy kid in class. Whenever you turn to look, they quickly stare at their desk. But when you turn back to your book, you can feel them peeking at you with a small smile. That little game means they want to be your friend.
kurals.university: The couplet builds on a chiastic play of nōkku (நோக்கு, ‘look’): yān nōkkum kālai (when I look) she looks at nilan (நிலன், the ground); nōkkākkāl (when I do not look) she looks and mella nakum (மெல்ல நகும், smiles gently). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take nakum as smiling or rejoicing to herself, and Kalaignar adds that this is a sign announcing her love. Commentators in the Parimelazhagar tradition treat the lowered gaze as nāṇam and the secret smile as the kurippu of consent. Pope: ‘I look on her: her eyes are on the ground the while: / I look away: she looks on me with timid smile.’ The two source sites agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When I was near, she could not look at me; / She smiled–but not to me–and half denied it.”
hinduism.explanation: King Dushyanta tells his friend how the shy Shakuntala avoided his eyes yet smiled in a way that half gave her away.
hinduism.tie_back: Avoiding his gaze while smiling is precisely the Kural’s picture of the beloved who looks down when watched and smiles when unwatched.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act II (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Project Gutenberg; near one-to-one on the averted look and the hidden smile.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, he standeth behind our wall, he looketh forth at the windows, shewing himself through the lattice.”
christianity.explanation: The beloved peers through the window lattice, watching while only half seen.
christianity.tie_back: Looking at the other from hiding is the game the Kural describes.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); it shares the half-hidden looking but not the downcast eyes or smile.

islam.quote_or_event: “And with them will be women limiting [their] glances, with large, [beautiful] eyes.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises the modest companions of paradise for restraining their gaze.
islam.tie_back: Lowered and restrained eyes as a mark of modesty is the same virtue the Kural sees in the beloved who looks at the ground.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified via the quran.com API; it matches the modest lowered gaze but not the secret smile.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Then she fell on her face, and bowed down to the ground, and said unto him: ‘Why have I found favour in thy sight, that thou shouldest take cognizance of me, seeing I am a foreigner?’”
judaism.explanation: Ruth bows to the ground before Boaz, wondering why he has noticed her kindly.
judaism.tie_back: Ruth lowers her eyes to the ground when Boaz notices her, and their story too ends in marriage.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; her bowing is gratitude more than shyness, so the fit is reasonable but partial.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that two bright qualities protect the world: hiri (a sense of shame) and ottappa (moral dread), without which people would not know any restraint.
buddhism.explanation: Modesty is honored in Buddhism as one of the guardians of the moral life.
buddhism.tie_back: The beloved’s lowered eyes show the same hiri the Buddha praises, even if the Kural’s setting is romantic.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified verbatim this session; only the modesty theme connects, so this is a next-best match.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Not to look at, nor to long for, not to think of, nor to praise, womankind: this is becoming the meditation of the noble ones.”
jainism.explanation: For the Jain monk, keeping the eyes from looking at women is part of the discipline of chastity.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism also values the downcast eye, but as a monk’s renunciation, not as a shy sign of love.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a contrasting match where the averted gaze serves renunciation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “And now both were fixing their eyes on the ground abashed, and again were throwing glances at each other, smiling with the light of love beneath their radiant brows.”
greek_mythology.explanation: At their secret meeting Medea and Jason look down in shyness, then steal smiling looks at each other.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Eyes on the ground, then a smiling glance: this is the Kural’s scene almost exactly.
greek_mythology.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 3.1022-1024 (tr. R. C. Seaton, 1912)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on theoi.com; near one-to-one.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle, discussing shame, cites the proverb that shame dwells in the eyes, which is why people feel it most before those who look at them.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, shame shows itself in how we meet or avoid another’s gaze.
philosophy.tie_back: The beloved who drops her eyes when looked at shows exactly this shame-in-the-eyes.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Rhetoric II.6, 1384a (tr. W. Rhys Roberts)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified verbatim this session; it explains the lowered gaze but not the smile.

adhikaram.english: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)

kurals.tamil:
குறிக்கொண்டு நோக்காமை அல்லால் ஒருகண்
சிறக்கணித்தாள் போல நகும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kurikkondu nokkaamai allaal orukan
sirakkaniththaal poala nagum.
kurals.meaning: She does not look straight at me; yet, as if narrowing one eye in a sidelong look, she smiles to herself.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes a friend pretends not to watch you, but you catch them looking out of the corner of their eye with a little grin. They are not really ignoring you; they are just being shy and playful.
kurals.university: Kuṟikkoṇṭu nōkkāmai (குறிக்கொண்டு நோக்காமை) is ‘not looking with a fixed aim’, that is, avoiding a direct gaze. The difficult word ciṟakkaṇittāḷ (சிறக்கணித்தாள்) is glossed by Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar as ‘narrowing one eye’ (oru kaṇṇaic curukki), while Puliyur Kesikan takes it as tilting one eye to one side; Pope’s ‘smiling side-long glance’ follows the second sense, and the explanatory gloss on ytamizh renders it as looking ‘with a half-closed eye’. Either way the commentators read the sidelong smile as a kurippu that she returns his love while seeming not to. The Tamil is the same on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Her glance was loving–but ’twas not for me; / Her step was slow–’twas grace, not coquetry.”
hinduism.explanation: The king tries to talk himself out of reading Shakuntala’s side glances as love, then admits that a lover reads every sign in his own favor.
hinduism.tie_back: The puzzle of whether an indirect glance means love is exactly the puzzle the Kural answers.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act II (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Project Gutenberg; it deals with reading indirect glances, though the king doubts rather than trusts them.

christianity.quote_or_event: “There be three things which are too wonderful for me, yea, four which I know not: The way of an eagle in the air; the way of a serpent upon a rock; the way of a ship in the midst of the sea; and the way of a man with a maid.”
christianity.explanation: The sage confesses that the hidden ways of love between a man and a woman are beyond his understanding.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s half-closed-eye smile is one of those mysterious ‘ways’ that only lovers can read.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); it speaks of love’s hidden signs in general, not of a sidelong glance.

islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes the companions of paradise as women who keep their gaze restrained.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s beloved likewise does not look straight at her lover, though her restraint hides a smile.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified via the quran.com API; only the restrained gaze matches, not the playful sidelong smile.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Behold, thou art fair, my love; behold, thou art fair; Thine eyes are as doves behind thy veil.”
judaism.explanation: The lover praises the beloved’s eyes glimpsed half-hidden behind her veil.
judaism.tie_back: Eyes that look out half-hidden recall the Kural’s narrowed, sidelong glance.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; a reasonable image match, with no smile.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Zen tradition’s Flower Sermon, the Buddha silently holds up a flower; only Mahakashyapa understands and answers with a smile, and the Buddha says the true teaching has passed to him.
buddhism.explanation: A wordless smile is shown as the sign of perfect understanding between two people.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a quiet smile carries a meaning that words do not.
buddhism.source: Wumenguan (The Gateless Gate), case 6, ‘The Buddha Holds Up a Flower’
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a later Chan/Zen story, not verified verbatim; the link is the meaningful silent smile, in a non-romantic setting.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A Sramana, engaged in penance, should not allow himself to watch the shape, beauty, coquetry, laughter, prattle, gestures, and glances of women, nor retain a recollection of them in his mind.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain monk is told not to dwell on the playful glances and laughter that the Kural celebrates.
jainism.tie_back: Jain scripture names the same playful glance and laughter as the Kural, but as things a renunciant must not watch.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; close in subject, opposite in valuation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “This honour she has from the beginning, and this is the portion allotted to her amongst men and undying gods, – the whisperings of maidens and smiles and deceits with sweet delight and love and graciousness.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod assigns to Aphrodite the realm of maidens’ whispers, smiles and playful deceits.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s sly half-smile, pretending not to look, belongs to exactly this province of Aphrodite.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on theoi.com; a good fit on playful smiles and pretense, without the specific glance.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Symposium, Diotima describes Eros as bold and resourceful, a clever hunter always weaving some scheme to win what is beautiful.
philosophy.explanation: Love, for Diotima, works by stratagem and indirection.
philosophy.tie_back: The beloved’s pretended indifference with a sidelong smile is one of love’s small stratagems.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified verbatim this session; only a loose thematic link to love’s indirection.

adhikaram.english: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)

kurals.tamil:
உறாஅ தவர்போல் சொலினும் செறாஅர்சொல்
ஒல்லை உணரப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Uraaa thavarpol solinum seraaarsol
ollai unarap padum.
kurals.meaning: Even when those who bear no anger speak as though they were strangers, the true meaning of their words is quickly understood.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes a friend says, ‘I don’t care, go away!’ but they are smiling and not really cross. You can tell right away they are only pretending. Kind people cannot hide their kindness for long.
kurals.university: Uṟāatavar (உறாஅதவர்) and ceṟāar (செறாஅர்) both carry the long-vowel extension (alapeṭai) used for metre: ‘those who are not intimate’ and ‘those who are not angry’. Ollai (ஒல்லை) means ‘quickly’. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses: though they speak outwardly like strangers without affection, the words of those with no enmity within are soon recognised; Solomon Pappaiah sets the scene with her reply ‘who are you?’ to his approach, and Kalaignar says the love she hides behind harsh words soon shows through. Puliyur Kesikan reads that the result (payan) of such words is soon felt. Pope: ‘Though with their lips affection they disown, / Yet, when they hate us not, ’tis quickly known.’ No variants on the two source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “She would not show her love for modesty, / Yet did not try so very hard to hide it.”
hinduism.explanation: King Dushyanta notes that Shakuntala hid her love out of modesty, but not so well that he could not see it.
hinduism.tie_back: Love that is outwardly hidden but quickly recognised is the Kural’s exact claim.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act II (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Project Gutenberg (second half of the stanza cited at Kural 1094); a strong thematic fit.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote unto you with many tears; not that ye should be grieved, but that ye might know the love which I have more abundantly unto you.”
christianity.explanation: Paul explains that his severe letter came from love, not from a wish to hurt.
christianity.tie_back: Words that sound hard but carry no enmity, and whose love is soon understood, are what the Kural describes.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); good on hard words from love, but not a lovers’ setting.

islam.quote_or_event: “I know when you are pleased with me or angry with me.” I said, “Whence do you know that?” He said, “When you are pleased with me, you say, ‘No, by the Lord of Muhammad,’ but when you are angry with me, then you say, ‘No, by the Lord of Abraham.’”
islam.explanation: The Prophet tells Aisha he can read her mood from the small way she words her oath, and she answers that even when cross she leaves only his name, not her love.
islam.tie_back: A spouse’s affection is read through the very words of a mock quarrel, as the Kural says it soon is.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; a strong, tender parallel on reading love beneath surface words.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; But the kisses of an enemy are importunate.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs teaches that hard treatment from a friend is trustworthy, while an enemy’s show of affection is false.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise says that harsh-sounding words from one who bears no anger are recognised for what they are.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; good on harshness without enmity, but not about lovers.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It’s through living together that a person’s virtue may be known, and then only after a long period, not a short period; by one who is attentive, not by one who is inattentive.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says a person’s true character is known only through long, attentive acquaintance.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism agrees that the inner heart can be read beneath appearances, though it says this takes long attention where the Kural says love is read quickly.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.192, Thana Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it shares the idea of reading the inner person but contrasts on speed, so it is a next-best match.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Having heard these well-spoken words of the virtuous lady, he returned to the Law like an elephant driven by the hook.”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati rebukes Rathanemi sharply, and he at once understands that her stern words were meant for his good.
jainism.tie_back: Severe words spoken without hatred are quickly understood, as the Kural says, though here they turn a man back to his vows rather than toward love.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a partial fit, using a genuine Jain story of Rajimati in a renunciant setting.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, Nausicaa asks her father for a wagon to wash clothes, too shy to speak of marriage, but Alcinous understands everything she has left unsaid and grants her request.
greek_mythology.explanation: A father reads his daughter’s unspoken wish beneath her ordinary words.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, the scene shows a hidden heart being understood at once through plain-sounding words.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified verbatim this session; strong on reading what is left unsaid, though not between lovers.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “There is no disguise which can long hide love where it exists, nor feign it where it does not.”
philosophy.explanation: La Rochefoucauld observes that real love always shows through any attempt to hide it.
philosophy.tie_back: This is nearly the Kural’s point: love behind stranger-like words is soon found out.
philosophy.source: La Rochefoucauld, Maxims 70 (tr. J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the Project Gutenberg text; near one-to-one.

adhikaram.english: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)

kurals.tamil:
செறாஅச் சிறுசொல்லும் செற்றார்போல் நோக்கும்
உறாஅர்போன்று உற்றார் குறிப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Seraaach chirusollum setraarpol nokkum
uraaarpondru utraar kurippu.
kurals.meaning: Small sharp words that carry no anger, and looks that seem hostile, are the signs of those who love while acting like strangers.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever seen two best friends tease each other, saying ‘You’re so annoying!’ while grinning? Their pretend-grumpy faces are really a sign of how close they are. Sometimes people who like each other act as if they don’t.
kurals.university: The couplet balances ceṟāac ciṟucol (செறாஅச் சிறுசொல், ‘little words that are not angry’) against ceṟṟār pōl nōkku (செற்றார்போல் நோக்கு, ‘a look like that of enemies’), and names both the kuṟippu of uṟṟār (உற்றார், intimates, lovers) who behave uṟāar pōnṟu (like those not intimate). Mu. Varadarasanar reads ciṟucol as kaṭuñcol, harsh words that hold no hostility; Kalaignar speaks of lovers ‘acting’ like strangers outwardly while loving within; Solomon Pappaiah frames it as the hero now understanding her earlier coldness. The couplet completes the thought of 1096 by naming the signs. Pope: ‘The slighting words that anger feign, while eyes their love reveal, / Are signs of those that love, but would their love conceal.’ Text identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Shakuntala (to herself): “I would never leave him if I could help myself.” … Shakuntala (aloud): “I am not your servant any longer. I will go when I like.”
hinduism.explanation: Shakuntala speaks sharply and threatens to leave, while privately admitting she cannot bear to go from the king’s presence.
hinduism.tie_back: Her cross words that hide affection are the Kural’s ‘little words without anger’ of a lover acting aloof.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act I (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Project Gutenberg (two lines from the same exchange, joined with an ellipsis); a strong dramatic parallel.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews teaches that God’s correction, though painful, is a sign of his love.
christianity.tie_back: Sternness that is really a sign of love is the Kural’s point, transposed from lovers to God and his children.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); only the idea of loving severity connects.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if We willed, We could show them to you, and you would know them by their mark; but you will surely know them by the tone of [their] speech.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says the Prophet would recognise people’s true inner state from the tone of their speech, whatever they say outwardly.
islam.tie_back: The Kural too says the inner heart is read from tone and look rather than from the literal words.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified via the quran.com API; it concerns exposing hidden hostility in hypocrites, the reverse of hidden love, so the match is on method only.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Joseph saw his brethren, and he knew them, but made himself strange unto them, and spoke roughly with them.”
judaism.explanation: Joseph recognises his brothers but treats them like strangers and speaks harshly, though he loves them and later weeps over them.
judaism.tie_back: Acting like a stranger and speaking roughly while loving within is exactly the Kural’s ‘intimates who seem like strangers’.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; near one-to-one on feigned strangeness hiding love, though between brothers.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Abhayarajakumara Sutta the Buddha says he will speak even unwelcome and disagreeable words if they are true and beneficial, comparing himself to a nurse who pulls a dangerous object from a baby’s throat even if it draws blood, out of compassion.
buddhism.explanation: Harsh-sounding speech can come from compassion rather than ill will.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s angerless sharp words, the Buddha’s hard words carry no hostility.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified verbatim this session; a good fit on harsh words without hostility, outside a romantic setting.

jainism.quote_or_event: “I am the daughter of the Bhoga-king, and you are an Andhakavrishni; being born in a noble family let us not become like Gandhana-snakes; firmly practise self-control!”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati speaks sternly to Rathanemi, not from hatred but to recall him to his vows.
jainism.tie_back: Her severe words without enmity resemble the Kural’s angerless sharp words, though their purpose is renunciation, not love.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified); a partial parallel in a contrasting setting.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus at last stands before Penelope, she treats him coolly as if he were a stranger, and Telemachus rebukes her hard heart; she answers that if he is truly Odysseus they will know each other by secret signs known only to the two of them.
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope’s apparent coldness hides a deep love that is waiting for its sign.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A beloved who acts like a stranger while loving within is the Kural’s exact picture.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified verbatim this session; a strong thematic fit.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch argues that a true friend’s frankness may sting like medicine while a flatterer’s sweetness harms, so the harshness of a friend should be read by its intent, not its surface.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch teaches how to tell real affection behind sharp words from false affection behind sweet ones.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural similarly says that sharp words without anger are a sign of real closeness.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the essay’s argument, not verified verbatim; it concerns friendship rather than love.

adhikaram.english: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)

kurals.tamil:
அசையியற்கு உண்டாண்டோர் ஏஎர்யான் நோக்கப்
பசையினள் பைய நகும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Asaiyiyarku undaandor eeryaan nokkap
pasaiyinal paiya nagum.
kurals.meaning: When I look at her imploringly, she softens and smiles gently; in that moment this delicate girl has a special grace.
kurals.elementary: When you look at someone with a hopeful, friendly face, and their serious look melts into a soft smile, it feels wonderful. That smile is a sign they are happy to be your friend.
kurals.university: Asaiyiyal (அசையியல்) is ‘she whose nature sways’, a soft, delicate girl; ēer (ஏஎர், ēr with alapeṭai) means beauty or grace, and āṇṭu (ஆண்டு) ‘then, there’. Pasaiyinaḷ (பசையினள்) is ‘she who has softened, become tender’. The commentators differ on ēer: Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it as a new beauty she has at that moment; Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan read the line as saying there is a sign (kuṟippu) or token of goodness in her smile; Kesikan also understands yān nōkka as ‘when I looked as if begging’. The ytamizh Sivayogi gloss reads differently again, showing real interpretive variety in this couplet. Pope: ‘I gaze, the tender maid relents the while; / And, oh the matchless grace of that soft smile!’ Text identical on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Shakuntala (to herself): “Oh, why do I have such feelings when I see this man? They seem wrong in a hermitage.”
hinduism.explanation: At her first sight of the king, Shakuntala feels her heart soften toward him and wonders at it.
hinduism.tie_back: Her heart softening at his look is the inner side of the Kural’s gentle, relenting smile.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act I (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Project Gutenberg; it shows her softening but not the smile.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then was I in his eyes as one that found favour.”
christianity.explanation: The beloved in the Song says that in her lover’s eyes she has found favour.
christianity.tie_back: Finding favour in the other’s eyes is the moment of mutual grace the Kural captures in the softened smile.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); reasonable on favour in the eyes, without the smile.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquility in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an names the affection and tenderness placed between spouses as one of God’s signs.
islam.tie_back: The softening tenderness (pasai) of the Kural’s beloved is the ‘affection and mercy’ the verse praises.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified via the quran.com API; a thematic fit on tender affection, not on the smile itself.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And it was so, when the king saw Esther the queen standing in the court, that she obtained favour in his sight; and the king held out to Esther the golden sceptre that was in his hand.”
judaism.explanation: When Esther appears before the king, his look softens and he extends his sceptre to her.
judaism.tie_back: A look that brings about a relenting, gracious response is the turn the Kural describes.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; the softening runs from king to queen, the reverse of the Kural, and is not romantic courtship.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigalovada Sutta the Buddha says a husband should honour his wife by courtesy and by not despising her, and that a wife who is so treated cares for him with love in return.
buddhism.explanation: Kindness offered is answered by kindness returned between partners.
buddhism.tie_back: The beloved’s softening in answer to his tender look is a small instance of this mutual courtesy.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified verbatim; a loose next-best match about married reciprocity.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasant things (by themselves) do not cause indifference nor emotions (as anger, &c.); but by either hating or loving them, a man undergoes such a change through delusion.”
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching says it is our own attachment, not the object, that stirs our emotions.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism would trace the delight the lover finds in her smile to his own attachment, offering a sober counterpoint to the Kural.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a contrasting next-best match.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Thus he spake, honouring her; and she cast her eyes down with a smile divinely sweet; and her soul melted within her, uplifted by his praise.”
greek_mythology.explanation: After Jason pleads with Medea as a suppliant, she looks down, smiles sweetly and melts toward him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A pleading look answered by a softened, gentle smile is the Kural’s scene exactly.
greek_mythology.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 3.1008-1010 (tr. R. C. Seaton, 1912)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on theoi.com; near one-to-one.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Phaedrus, Socrates says the beloved, receiving the lover’s devoted gaze, comes to feel a returning love (anteros), an image of love reflected back, though he hardly knows what it is.
philosophy.explanation: Love given through the eyes calls forth love in return.
philosophy.tie_back: The beloved’s softening smile under the lover’s gaze is this returning love made visible.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified verbatim this session; a good thematic fit.

adhikaram.english: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)

kurals.tamil:
ஏதிலார் போலப் பொதுநோக்கு நோக்குதல்
காதலார் கண்ணே உள.
kurals.transliteration:
Edhilaar polap podhunokku nokkudhal
kaadhalaar kanne ula.
kurals.meaning: To look at each other with a plain, ordinary look, as if they were strangers, is a habit found only among those who are in love.
kurals.elementary: Two good friends might act normal in front of everyone, as if they hardly know each other, but they still understand each other perfectly. Only close friends can play that ‘we’re just strangers’ game.
kurals.university: Ētilār (ஏதிலார்) means ‘strangers, people with no connection’, and potu nōkku (பொதுநோக்கு) is a ‘common’ or neutral look, the kind one gives anyone in a crowd. Kātalār kaṇṇē uḷa (காதலார் கண்ணே உள) asserts, with the emphatic -ē, that this is found only among lovers. Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as lovers outwardly looking like strangers while loving within; Kalaignar specifies that they do this in public places; Puliyur Kesikan applies it to both lovers looking at each other. The couplet draws a general rule from the hero’s experience in 1096-1098. Pope: ‘The look indifferent, that would its love disguise, / Is only read aright by lovers’ eyes.’ Text identical on both source sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Although she does not speak to me, / She listens while I speak; / Her eyes turn not to see my face, / But nothing else they seek.”
hinduism.explanation: The king observes that Shakuntala seems not to look at him or speak to him, yet her whole attention is on him.
hinduism.tie_back: An outwardly indifferent look that hides full attention is the Kural’s lovers’ ‘stranger’s look’.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act I (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Project Gutenberg; strong parallel on studied outward indifference.

christianity.quote_or_event: “O that thou wert as my brother, that sucked the breasts of my mother! when I should find thee without, I would kiss thee; yea, I should not be despised.”
christianity.explanation: The beloved wishes she could show her affection openly in public without reproach, as one may with a brother.
christianity.tie_back: Because lovers must look like mere acquaintances in public, the Kural says their neutral looks are a sign of love.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); a strong fit on lovers hiding affection in public.

islam.quote_or_event: “An ignorant [person] would think them self-sufficient because of their restraint, but you will know them by their [characteristic] sign.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says that the dignified poor hide their need, but the perceptive recognise them by their sign.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the outward look misleads others, while the one who knows reads the hidden sign.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified via the quran.com API; the shared idea is reading a hidden state behind restraint, not love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Esther had not made known her people nor her kindred; for Mordecai had charged her that she should not tell it. And Mordecai walked every day before the court of the women’s house, to know how Esther did.”
judaism.explanation: Esther and Mordecai hide their close bond in public, yet he watches over her every day.
judaism.tie_back: Two people who behave like strangers in public while staying deeply bound is the pattern the Kural describes.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; a good fit on a concealed bond, though it is family love, not romance.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Dhammapada commentary, Patacara, a rich man’s daughter, falls in love with a household servant and hides the bond from her family until the two secretly leave together.
buddhism.explanation: A hidden love, kept from others’ eyes, is part of the background of the nun Patacara’s story.
buddhism.tie_back: Lovers concealing their bond in front of others reflects the Kural’s ‘stranger’s look’, though the Buddhist story leads to grief and renunciation.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada Commentary on verse 113 (story of Patacara)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified verbatim; a loose next-best match.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though those who possess the three Guptis, cannot be disturbed even by well-adorned goddesses, still it is recommended to monks to live by themselves, as this is wholesome in every way.”
jainism.explanation: The disciplined monk remains outwardly and inwardly unmoved even before great beauty.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain monk’s unmoved look is genuine composure, while the Kural’s lovers only pretend to be unmoved, a telling contrast.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a contrasting next-best match.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “No relatives had guessed their secret love, / for all their converse was by nods and signs.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Pyramus and Thisbe keep their love hidden from their families by speaking only through nods and signs.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Outsiders see nothing, but the lovers understand each other perfectly, which is the Kural’s point.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on theoi.com; a Roman retelling of a Greek-setting myth, closely matching hidden lovers’ signs.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal writes that the heart has its reasons which reason does not know.
philosophy.explanation: For Pascal, the heart perceives and acts on things that detached reasoning cannot see.
philosophy.tie_back: Lovers’ seemingly neutral looks carry a meaning that only the heart, not an observer’s reasoning, can read.
philosophy.source: Blaise Pascal, Pensées 277 (Brunschvicg numbering; tr. W. F. Trotter)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous line, not verified verbatim this session; a loose thematic link.

adhikaram.english: Recognition of the Signs (of Mutual Love)

kurals.tamil:
கண்ணொடு கண்இணை நோக்கொக்கின் வாய்ச்சொற்கள்
என்ன பயனும் இல.
kurals.transliteration:
Kannodu kaninai nokkokkin vaaichchorkal
enna payanum ila.
kurals.meaning: When eye meets eye and the looks agree, the words of the mouth are of no use at all.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes you and your best friend just look at each other and both burst out laughing, because you are thinking the same thing. You didn’t need to say a single word. Your eyes did all the talking.
kurals.university: Kaṇṇoṭu kaṇ iṇai nōkku okkin (கண்ணொடு கண்இணை நோக்கொக்கின்): ‘if the pair of eyes agree in look with the other pair’. Okkin (‘if they match’) is the key word: mutual, matching love, not one-sided longing. Vāyccoṟkaḷ (வாய்ச்சொற்கள்) are words of the mouth, which then have enna payanum ila, ‘no use whatever’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss: when eyes join in equal love, spoken words become unnecessary; Puliyur Kesikan specifies the two who are united in kāmam. The couplet closes the chapter by stating its principle: in love, the eyes are the true language, which is why the whole chapter has been about reading looks. Pope: ‘When eye to answering eye reveals the tale of love, / All words that lips can say must useless prove.’ The ytamizh transliteration writes kaN-inai, matching the Tamil கண்இணை; the text is identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Why, the good king shows his love for her in his tender glances, and he has been wasting away, as if he were losing sleep.”
hinduism.explanation: Shakuntala’s friend says the king’s love is already plain from his glances, before he has said anything.
hinduism.tie_back: Love declared through the eyes, making words unnecessary, is the Kural’s point.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act III (tr. Arthur W. Ryder, 1912)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Project Gutenberg; it shows glances revealing love, though one-sidedly and through a third person.

christianity.quote_or_event: “My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth.”
christianity.explanation: John teaches that real love is shown in what is done rather than in what is said.
christianity.tie_back: Both the epistle and the Kural place true love beyond mere words of the mouth.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV); it shares the ‘beyond words’ idea, but speaks of deeds rather than looks.

islam.quote_or_event: “Souls are like recruited troops: Those who are like qualities are inclined to each other, but those who have dissimilar qualities, differ.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that kindred souls recognise and are drawn to each other.
islam.tie_back: Two hearts that ‘agree’ at a glance, needing no words, is the instant recognition the hadith describes.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; a good fit on wordless mutual recognition, not specifically romantic.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.”
judaism.explanation: At their first meeting Jonathan’s soul becomes bound to David’s.
judaism.tie_back: An instant union of souls that needs no long speeches matches the Kural’s agreement of the eyes.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; strong on instant union of hearts, but it is friendship and does not mention the eyes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If both husband & wife want to see one another not only in the present life but also in the life to come, they should be in tune [with each other] in conviction, in tune in virtue, in tune in generosity, and in tune in discernment.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells a devoted couple that being in tune with each other in deeper qualities is what keeps them together.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s matching looks are a sign of the same deep agreement between two people.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.55, Samajivina Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; strong on mutual agreement between partners, without the eyes-over-words point.

jainism.quote_or_event: Rajimati was betrothed to Arishtanemi, who renounced the world on the way to their wedding; without any further exchange of words between them, she cut her hair and followed him into the ascetic life, and both reached perfection.
jainism.explanation: Rajimati’s devotion to Arishtanemi is shown by following his path, not by speeches.
jainism.tie_back: Jain narrative gives a love so in tune that words are unnecessary, though it ends in shared renunciation rather than union.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.27-30, 48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45); cf. the Nemidutakavya noted by Jacobi
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase checked against the Jacobi text on sacred-texts.com; a genuine Jain love story, but the parallel to eyes replacing words is loose.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “So they two stood face to face without a word, without a sound, like oaks or lofty pines, which stand quietly side by side on the mountains when the wind is still.”
greek_mythology.explanation: When Medea and Jason meet in secret, they stand facing each other in silence, already joined in love.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Face to face with no words needed is the Kural’s final image.
greek_mythology.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 3.967-970 (tr. R. C. Seaton, 1912)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on theoi.com; strong on silent mutual presence, though words do follow.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “There is no less eloquence in the voice, in the eyes and in the air of a speaker than in his choice of words.”
philosophy.explanation: La Rochefoucauld notes that the eyes and manner speak as eloquently as words.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural goes further, saying that when the eyes agree, words are not needed at all.
philosophy.source: La Rochefoucauld, Maxims 249 (tr. J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the Project Gutenberg text; a reasonable fit, not about lovers.
